0.title: Faith That Works: The Letter of James
0.overview:
James is the most practical book in the New Testament — and one of the most misunderstood. Martin Luther famously called it “an epistle of straw,” contrasting its apparent emphasis on works with Paul’s gospel of grace. He was wrong — his polemical situation against Roman Catholic merit theology made him over-read James as a rival to Paul rather than as his complement. Read on its own terms, James is not a rival to the gospel of grace but its most searching ethical application: what does genuine, living, gospel-produced faith actually look like? The answer is not passive and invisible. It looks like patience in trials, generosity to the poor, a bridled tongue, peaceful wisdom, and prayer that moves heaven.

The author identifies himself as “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). The most natural identification is James the brother of Jesus, the leader of the Jerusalem church, the man who had not believed in Jesus during his earthly ministry (John 7:5) but was transformed by a resurrection appearance (1 Cor 15:7) into the pillar of the first church (Gal 2:9) and its martyred leader (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9). The letter was probably written before the Jerusalem Council of AD 49, making it possibly the earliest New Testament letter — which means James was wrestling with the application of the gospel to practical life before Paul had written most of his letters.

The letter draws deeply on the Sermon on the Mount, which James had presumably heard from Jesus himself, and on the Old Testament wisdom tradition — Proverbs, Job, the Psalms of lament. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” — Jewish Christians scattered beyond Palestine, probably after the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1). These were people under pressure: economic hardship, social marginalization, the temptation to compromise, the fracturing of community under stress.

James’s relationship to Paul is complementary, not contradictory. Paul says Abraham was justified by faith (Rom 4); James says Abraham was justified by works (Jas 2:21). The difference is not in the content of justification but in its reference point: Paul speaks of justification before God in the court of heaven (the forensic verdict of “righteous” that comes through faith alone); James speaks of justification before men in the arena of visible life (the demonstration that faith is genuine, which appears in its works). Both agree that dead faith saves no one; both agree that living faith produces fruit. Paul says faith alone justifies; James says the faith that justifies is never alone.

Read James as the letter that will not let you be comfortable with a merely intellectual Christianity. It asks the hardest questions: Does your faith survive under pressure? Does it make you generous? Does it control your tongue? Does it make you humble? Does it make you pray? These are not questions about earning salvation but about whether what you call faith is the real thing. James is not offering a second route to justification; he is describing what justification produces in the life of the one who has genuinely received it. It produces the kind of faith that works — which is the only kind that is faith at all.

1.title: Tested and Proven: Trials, Wisdom, and the Word
1.overview:
Chapter 1 sets out the letter’s concern: real faith under pressure. James starts with circumstance, not doctrine. His readers are in trials, and in God’s hands trials produce what nothing else can: tested faith, steadfastness and maturity.

Three threads run through the chapter: trials and the faith they prove (vv. 2–12); temptation, which comes from our own desires, not from God, the unchanging giver of every good gift (vv. 13–18); and the word of God, which gives new birth, must be done and not only heard, and produces pure religion (vv. 19–27). The key word is “perfect” or “complete” (vv. 4, 17, 25): not flawless, but whole. Its opposite is the double-minded man (v. 8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Trials, Wisdom, and the God Who Does Not Change
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James, a servant of Christ, writes to scattered believers. Count trials joy, because tested faith produces steadfastness and maturity. If you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously, but ask without being double-minded. Poor and rich alike should boast in what God has made them. The one who endures will receive the crown of life. God never tempts anyone; temptation comes from our own desire and ends in death. But every good gift comes from the unchanging Father of lights, who gave us new birth by the word of truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing and Tempting

God tests to prove and strengthen; he never tempts. Temptation comes from our own desire, while every good gift comes from the Father of lights, who does not change.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were scattered believers under real pressure and real poverty.

Now: Counting trials joy is a judgment about what they produce, and it can be made while we are still in pain.

verseByVerse.quote: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: Greetings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, greets the scattered people of God.

Who writes. Almost certainly James the brother of Jesus (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19), leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15). He grew up in the same house as Jesus, yet calls himself only a “slave”.

From unbelief to “Lord”. During Jesus’ ministry his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5), and once came to take him home, thinking he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Then the risen Christ “appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7). The man who thought his brother mad now calls him Lord.

The Dispersion. Jewish believers scattered by persecution (Acts 8:1; 11:19). These are refugees. The trials, the poverty and the cheated labourers in this letter are real.

For worship. Only the resurrection explains a brother worshipping his brother. James’s life is evidence that Jesus rose.
verseByVerse.note: James was most likely the brother of Jesus, who came to faith after the resurrection and led the Jerusalem church. He was put to death about AD 62. “The Dispersion” means Jewish believers scattered outside the land of Israel. The letter echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider it pure joy when you face trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. Let steadfastness finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, lacking nothing.

Count, not feel. The verb is an accounting word: reckon, evaluate. James is not commanding an emotion, which no one can produce on demand. He is commanding a judgment about what trials are, and that can be made while you are still hurting.

When, not if. “Meet” means to fall into unexpectedly, like the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10:30).

For you know. The joy is informed. Testing is the assayer’s word for proving metal genuine. What it produces is hypomonē, the strength to remain under a weight, which can be made in no other way.

Let it finish. The process can be cut short: by escaping, numbing or growing bitter.

Perfect. Teleios: complete, mature, not sinless.

On a Tuesday. A woman’s long illness has stripped away her strength and plans. She does not feel joyful. But she can say, “Lord, I believe you are using this to make me more like Christ.” That is counting it joy.

verseByVerse.quote: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given. But ask in faith, without doubting, because the doubter is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.

Wisdom for the trial. In the middle of a trial you cannot see what it is doing or what to do next. Biblical wisdom is practical: what to do on Tuesday.

Generously, without reproach. God gives simply, without calculating. And he does not sigh or remind you that you asked last month.

What “doubting” does not mean. Not the struggle of a believer who finds faith hard. The man who said, “I believe; help my unbelief” was answered (Mark 9:24). The word means divided within oneself.

A wave. Not a stone sinking, but something with no fixed position, pushed wherever the wind blows: wanting God’s wisdom on Sunday and the world’s on Monday.

verseByVerse.quote: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord; he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such a person should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. He is double-minded and unstable in everything he does.

Double-minded. Dipsychos, “two-souled”, a word James seems to have coined. Not a man who disbelieves, but one with two centres of loyalty, both real, pulling different ways. He prays sincerely and hedges sincerely.

The letter’s disease. Faith without works (2:14), blessing and cursing from one mouth (3:10), friendship with God and the world (4:4): every section applies this word. The remedy comes at 4:8: “purify your hearts, you double-minded.”

Why nothing? Not because God is petty. A man who asks for wisdom while keeping his options open has not really asked. He wants a second opinion to weigh against others.

On a Tuesday. Before praying about a decision, ask yourself: have I already decided what I will do if God’s answer goes the wrong way? If so, confess it. Then ask with an undivided heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poor believer should take pride in his high position, and the rich in his humiliation, because he will fade like a wild flower. The sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its flower falls and its beauty is gone. So the rich will fade away even while they go about their business.

A crossing. The poor believer is told to boast in his exaltation: he is a child of God, an heir. His social position is the least true thing about him. The rich believer boasts in being brought low: he came to God with empty hands like everyone else.

The flower. After the rains Palestinian hills turn green, then the desert wind browns them in a day (Isaiah 40:6–8).

In the midst of his pursuits. Not after he has finished, but with the diary full, like the man building bigger barns (Luke 12:16–21).

On a Tuesday. A believer who earns little feels small at a church where others drive new cars. James tells her what she really is. And he tells the man with the new car to hold it loosely: he is grass.

parallels.desc: The grass withers, the flower fades

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the one who endures trials, because after passing the test he will receive the crown of life God has promised to those who love him.

Stood the test. The assayer’s word, now a verdict: proven genuine.

The crown of life. The victor’s wreath, and the crown is life itself.

Promised to those who love him. It rests on a promise, not on impressive endurance. And it is for those who love God. Steadfastness is what love looks like under weight. Endurance without love is mere stubbornness.

A hinge. The word for trial is the same as for temptation. One circumstance can be God’s test and our desire’s opportunity.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me”, because God cannot be tempted by evil and does not tempt anyone. Each person is tempted when dragged away and enticed by his own desire. Desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin, when full-grown, gives birth to death.

The old excuse. He made me this way; he put it in front of me. James answers: there is nothing in God for evil to appeal to, and he tempts no one.

Test and temptation. God does test (Genesis 22:1). The same Greek root covers both. A test aims to prove and strengthen; a temptation aims to destroy. The difference lies in who uses the circumstance for what.

Lured and baited. Hunting and fishing words: dragged from cover, drawn by bait. “His own desire”: the bait works because of what is already in the fish.

Conception to death. Desire conceives, sin is born, sin grows, death is delivered. At every stage it looks manageable. James lays out the whole line so that you can see the end from the beginning.

What it does not mean. Being tempted is not sin. Jesus was tempted “yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Sin begins when desire is welcomed and cherished, when it “conceives”. And “lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13) asks God to keep us from trials that would overwhelm us, not to stop him from tempting us.

On a Tuesday. A man notices a thought about a colleague. The thought is not yet sin. The moment he welcomes it, it begins to grow. He turns away, prays, and changes what he is doing. A temptation resisted is a victory.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived. Every good and perfect gift comes from above, from the Father of lights, who does not change like shifting shadows. By his own will he gave us new birth through the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creation.

Only good comes down. The lie that God is behind our temptation is a deception, and James corrects it by describing God.

Father of lights. The maker of sun, moon and stars, which constantly change. He does not. No season, no eclipse, no moods.

Why it matters in trials. The temptation is not usually to doubt God exists, but to suspect he has gone cool. The light does not flicker.

Brought forth. A birth word, answering v. 15. Desire gives birth to sin and death; God gives birth to life. The initiative is his: “of his own will”. The means is “the word of truth”, the gospel (Ephesians 1:13; 1 Peter 1:23).

Firstfruits. The first sheaf of the harvest, a real portion and a promise of more. Believers are the first instalment of a renewed creation.

For worship. List the good gifts of today, the small ones too, and trace each back up to the Father who does not change.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger, because human anger does not produce God’s righteousness. Put off moral filth and humbly receive the word planted in you, which can save you. Do not only hear the word but do it. The hearer who does nothing is like a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face; the doer who keeps looking into the law of liberty is blessed. Religion that cannot control the tongue is worthless. Pure religion is caring for orphans and widows and keeping oneself unstained by the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mirror

Hearing without doing is self-deception. The blessed man looks into the perfect law of liberty, stays there, and acts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Orphans and widows were the people with no one to speak for them.

Now: Pure religion still means turning up for the helpless and keeping unstained from the world — both, not one.

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My dear brothers and sisters, be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteousness God desires.

Receiving the word. In context (vv. 18, 21), James is first describing how to receive Scripture, then how to treat each other.

Three habits. Quick to hear: leaning in. Slow to speak: not silence, but order. Slow to anger: not never angry, but slow, as God himself is (Exodus 34:6).

What anger cannot do. James does not say the anger is unjustified. These refugees had real grievances. He says it will not produce what it aims at. It feels like the engine of righteousness, and is not.

On a Tuesday. A heated online thread about a church issue. Before typing, read the other person’s whole post twice. Wait an hour. Then, if you still need to, reply gently.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So get rid of all moral filth and the evil that is so common, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save you.

Take off, take in. “Put away” is the word for removing dirty clothes. You cannot receive the word while wearing them.

With meekness. Strength that has stopped fighting back. Come to Scripture without a case to argue, letting it have the last word.

The implanted word. Already sown in them by God (Jeremiah 31:33). Their task is to let it grow.

Able to save. Not just inform or improve. James, often called a moralist, grounds his whole ethic in a word planted by God that saves.

verseByVerse.quote: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not merely listen to the word, deceiving yourselves. Do what it says.

The letter’s thesis. James does not belittle hearing; he has just commanded it. The problem is hearing only.

Doers. A noun of character: someone who is a doer.

Self-deception. The word is from accounting: to miscalculate. Not hypocrisy, which deceives others, but getting the sum wrong about yourself. The hearer has felt moved and agreed warmly, and files the feeling as obedience.

A religious danger. The more sermons we hear, the more familiar being moved becomes, and the easier it is to mistake for change.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who hears the word but does not do it is like someone who looks carefully at his face in a mirror, then walks away and immediately forgets what he looks like.

He looked intently. He is not careless in the moment. He is engaged.

The failure is afterwards. He looked, he left, and it was gone at once.

What mirrors are for. Not admiration but diagnosis: to see the smudge you cannot see without help. Their value lies in what you do in the ten seconds after you turn away. The mirror worked perfectly; the information did not survive the walk to the door, like a sermon between church and car park.

On a Tuesday. After a sermon, write one sentence: “This week I will…” Then tell someone. It turns a mirror into a change.

verseByVerse.quote: But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever looks intently into the perfect law that gives freedom, and keeps on looking, not forgetting what he has heard but doing it, will be blessed in what he does.

Looks into. To stoop and peer in, as Peter and John bent to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5).

The law of liberty. Not the law as a way to earn acceptance; James has just said the word saves. It is God’s revealed will, kept now as a freed man, not as a slave earning his release.

Perseveres. Stays bent over it. The difference between the two men is not how well they looked, but that one stayed.

Blessed in his doing. Not paid for it afterwards. The blessing is inside the obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who thinks he is religious but does not control his tongue deceives himself, and his religion is worthless. Pure and faultless religion before God the Father is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

Worthless religion. Applied not to an unbeliever but to a churchgoer with a loose mouth. Of all disqualifiers, James chose speech, a sin most churches tolerate.

Two things, joined. Care for the defenceless and personal holiness. People often prefer one. James joins them with “and”.

Visit. Orphans and widows had no one to speak for them. “Visit” is the word used of God visiting his people. It means turning up, not sending money from a distance.

Today. Fostering and adoption, supporting single mothers, visiting the lonely elderly, caring for widows in the church. And keeping unstained means refusing the world’s greed, pride, view of sex and contempt for the weak (4:4; 1 John 2:15–17).

What it does not mean. James is not defining all of religion or dismissing doctrine; he knew what he believed (2:19). He is naming the test.

On a Tuesday. Ask: has anyone who has nothing to offer me seen me lately? Then go and see them.

2.title: No Partiality: Faith That Sees Every Person
2.overview:
Chapter 2 has two movements, closely linked. The first (vv. 1–13) confronts favouritism in the church: welcoming the rich visitor to a good seat and sending the poor man to the floor. The second (vv. 14–26) asks what real faith is: a faith that produces no works is dead. The link is the poor visitor. A faith that produces no love for him is exactly the dead faith of vv. 14–26.

James is not opposing Paul’s gospel. He is opposing a counterfeit of it: the idea that agreeing with correct doctrine is the same as saving faith. Even demons believe that God is one. What saves is living faith in Christ, shown in Abraham offering Isaac and Rahab sheltering the spies. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Gold Ring and the Royal Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not hold faith in the glorious Lord Jesus while showing favouritism. James stages a scene: a man with a gold ring is given a good seat, a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand or sit on the floor. That makes you corrupt judges. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while the rich oppress you. Favouritism breaks the royal law of love, and breaking one command makes you guilty before the one Lawgiver. So speak and act as those who will be judged, for mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Lawgiver

Partiality contradicts faith in the Lord of glory and breaks the royal law. Whoever fails at one point stands guilty before the one who spoke the whole law — and mercy triumphs over judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The congregation seated the man with the gold ring well and the poor man on the floor.

Now: The sin is not only exclusion but ranking people inside a real welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My brothers and sisters, as believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favouritism.

Partiality. The word means “receiving the face”: judging by appearance. Its background is the courtroom, where the law forbade judges to favour rich or poor (Leviticus 19:15).

Against the faith. Favouritism is not bad manners but a contradiction of what they believe.

The Lord of glory. Literally “our Lord Jesus Christ, the glory”: the highest thing James says of his brother. Beside that glory, the gap between a gold ring and rags is nothing.

Who writes. James watched Jesus grow up in Nazareth, where there was no glory to see and no family standing. He knew appearances mislead.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,” have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suppose a man with gold rings and fine clothes comes into your meeting, and a poor man in filthy clothes comes in too. If you give special attention to the rich man, “Sit here in a good seat”, but tell the poor man, “Stand there” or “Sit on the floor by my feet”, have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil motives?

The scene. The gold ring was a mark of rank in Roman society. His clothes are literally “shining”. The poor man’s are filthy, because he has nothing else.

Nobody is thrown out. The poor man is welcomed and seated, on the floor. The sin is not exclusion but ranking, inside a genuine welcome. That is why it is so recognisable.

Divided. “Made distinctions” is the root of “doubting” in 1:6. The double-mindedness of chapter 1 shows itself in the seating.

On a Tuesday. A church greets the well-dressed couple warmly and asks them to join the welcome team, while the man who smells of alcohol is politely ignored after the service. Ask whom you sat beside last Sunday, and why.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen: has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him? But you have dishonoured the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court, and blaspheme the noble name by which you are called?

God’s choice. Not that poverty qualifies anyone, or that every poor person is saved. It is how God has actually worked (1 Corinthians 1:26–29). God chooses the very people this church seats on the floor.

The irony. The rich they flatter are the class that exploits them, sues them and insults Christ, whose name was spoken over them at baptism.

What it does not mean. Not that the rich cannot be saved, and not a call to favour the poor instead; v. 1 forbids partiality either way. James exposes the folly of fawning on people because of a ring.

verseByVerse.quote: If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you really keep the royal law in Scripture, “Love your neighbour as yourself”, you are doing well. But if you show favouritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.

The defence. Someone says: we were being hospitable. James grants the standard: love your neighbour (Leviticus 19:18), which sits three verses after the ban on partiality (19:15).

The trap closes. Loving your neighbour as yourself leaves no room for ranking. Whichever man you seated well, you did not treat the other as yourself. Partiality is not a lesser love but the contradiction of love.

Transgressors. The would-be judges are now in the dock.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at one point is guilty of breaking all of it. The one who said, “Do not commit adultery”, also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have broken the law.

One lawgiver. The law is not a list of separate rules from which you may keep most. It is the expression of one person’s will. A window with one hole in it is a broken window.

The pointed examples. Adultery and murder were the sins they would condemn most readily. James puts seating the poor man on the floor in the same sentence.

What it does not mean. Not that all sins are equally serious in their effects; Scripture weighs them differently. The point is that every sin sets us against the same God, and no amount of law-keeping makes up for the part broken. That is why we need Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speak and act as those who will be judged by the law that gives freedom, because judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

Law of liberty. As in 1:25: God’s will kept by people already accepted. But the freed are still judged for how they lived in that freedom.

No mercy for the merciless. Jesus’ own teaching (Matthew 18:21–35; 6:12). A merciless person is not disqualified for failing to earn mercy. He is exposed: mercy received always produces mercy given.

Mercy triumphs. The verb means to exult over a defeated opponent. Judgment is real; mercy is stronger.

On a Tuesday. You remember the cruel thing your sister said years ago. Remember how much mercy God has shown you. Then pick up the phone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What good is it to say you have faith if you have no works? Can that kind of faith save? Words of blessing to a hungry brother with no food given are useless; faith without works is dead. Even demons believe that God is one, and tremble. Abraham was counted righteous when he believed, and his faith was shown and completed when he offered Isaac. Rahab’s faith was shown when she hid the spies. As the body without breath is dead, so faith without works is dead.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith That Works

James asks whether a faith that is only said can save. Abraham was counted righteous by faith, and his obedience showed that faith to be alive. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the demons believe that God is one — and shudder.

Now: Warm words to a hungry brother with nothing given are the picture of dead faith.

verseByVerse.quote: What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What good is it, brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but has no works? Can that faith save him?

Two small words. “Says”: James describes a man who claims faith. And “that faith”: the Greek has the article, “the faith”, the kind just described. The question expects the answer no.

Paul and James. Paul answers, “How is a sinner justified?” By faith, apart from works of the law. James answers, “What kind of faith justifies?” The living kind, which works. Paul’s “works” are law-works done to gain standing; James’s are the fruit of a changed life, starting with a coat for someone cold. Paul writes against adding works to Christ; James against those who have subtracted them and are comfortable.

Living or dead. James never sets faith against works. He sets living faith against dead faith. Works are faith’s vital signs.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says we are justified by faith, not works; James says a faith that produces no works is not saving faith. They answer different errors.

verseByVerse.quote: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a brother or sister has no clothes and no food for the day, and one of you says, “Go in peace; keep warm and eat well”, but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is that? In the same way, faith by itself, without works, is dead.

Daily food. Not lack of comfort: nothing to eat today. And not a stranger, but someone in the church.

Correct words. “Go in peace” was the ordinary blessing; the verbs may even be a prayer. He has said everything and done nothing. Silence would be less offensive.

Fluent religion. James could have chosen adultery or theft to expose hollow faith. He chose a coat and a meal: religion that is warm, fluent and costs nothing.

Dead. Not weak or immature, but dead. A corpse is not a person with reduced vitality.

What it does not mean. Not that weak or inconsistent works prove your faith dead. James says “we all stumble in many ways” (3:2). Living faith may be small and imperfect, but it is real: it trusts Christ, struggles against sin, and shows itself, however feebly, in love.

On a Tuesday. You tell a struggling colleague, “I’ll pray for you.” Do pray. Then ask if you can drop round a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Someone will say, “You have faith; I have works.” Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one. Good! Even the demons believe that, and shudder.

The objection. Probably: faith and works are different gifts for different people.

Unanswerable. Faith is invisible. It can only be shown by what it does.

The Shema. “God is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), recited by every Jew daily. James grants it: you do well. Right belief matters.

The demons. They are perfect monotheists, and in the Gospels they name Jesus correctly before anyone else. And they shudder, hair standing on end. Right creed, real feelings, and no salvation, because they will not trust and obey.

A searching verse. For anyone whose Christianity is correct convictions plus feeling moved in a service, James has just described that combination and named who else has it.
verseByVerse.note: The confession “God is one” is the Shema, the daily creed of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?
verseByVerse.commentary:
You foolish person, do you want evidence that faith without works is useless?

Empty. “Foolish” means hollow. His faith is empty, and so is he.

Useless. Idle, out of work, like a field lying fallow. Perhaps a play on words: faith without works does not work. James leaves no room for a faith that is real but merely lacks an optional extra.

verseByVerse.quote: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Was not our father Abraham justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith and his actions were working together, and his faith was made complete by what he did.

The hard sentence. It troubled Luther: James uses Abraham, Paul’s great example of faith (Romans 4), and seems to say the opposite.

Chronology. Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15:6, when he believed God’s promise. He offered Isaac in Genesis 22, decades later. The offering cannot have made him righteous; he had been righteous for years.

Working together, completed. Faith was the active partner, and it was “completed”: brought to maturity, as a seed is fulfilled in a tree. Isaac was the very promise Abraham had believed. Only a man who truly trusted God could raise that knife.

Two senses of “justify”. Paul means declared righteous before God. James means shown to be righteous, vindicated, as Jesus said “wisdom is justified by her deeds” (Matthew 11:19).

verseByVerse.quote: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness”, and he was called God’s friend. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.

James quotes Genesis 15:6. The very verse Paul builds on. The statement that Abraham was counted righteous by believing stands. Genesis 22 “fulfilled” it, as a prophecy is fulfilled: the faith of chapter 15 proved real in chapter 22.

Friend of God. The offering produced not merit but intimacy (Isaiah 41:8).

“Not by faith alone”. The only place in the New Testament with the phrase, and it is negated. But James denies justification by a faith that is alone, unaccompanied: the merely spoken faith of v. 14.

The Roman Catholic reading. Roman Catholic teaching cites this verse for justification as a process to which faith and works both contribute. But James is not describing how a sinner is first accepted; he quotes Genesis 15:6 to say Abraham was counted righteous when he believed, then shows how that faith proved true. The Reformers’ formula holds: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

For worship. The God who declares sinners righteous for Christ’s sake also makes them his friends.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, many years before he offered Isaac in Genesis 22; the offering showed the faith was real.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she welcomed the spies and sent them away by another road? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.

The opposite example. Abraham: patriarch, Jew, friend of God. Rahab: Gentile, woman, prostitute. Between them they cover everyone. And in a chapter on partiality, the church that seats people by their clothes is shown someone God justified whom they would not have let through the door.

Her act. Treason against her city, done on the strength of what she believed about Israel’s God (Joshua 2:11). Hebrews 11:31 credits it to faith. Two sides of one event.

Her lie. She lied to the king’s men (Joshua 2:4–5). James commends her siding with God’s people at risk of her life, not the lie as such. Christians differ on whether deceiving those bent on murder is sin; the more likely view is that her lie was a sin forgiven, and her faith was what God honoured.

Body and breath. Faith is the body; works are the breath. Breath does not matter more than the body, but it proves there is life. A faith with no works is a corpse: all the features recognisable, and nothing moving.

On a Tuesday. Ask, not “Do I believe the right things?” but “Is my faith breathing?” Look for the small signs: a kindness done, a sin resisted, a gift given. Then thank God for the life they show.

3.title: The Tongue and True Wisdom
3.overview:
Chapter 3 deals with two linked themes: the tongue and wisdom. The tongue (vv. 1–12) is small but decisive, like a bit, a rudder or a spark, and no human can tame it. Its problem is not speech but the heart: a spring gives what its source supplies.

So James turns to wisdom (vv. 13–18). Earthly wisdom, full of jealousy and selfish ambition, produces disorder. Wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, merciful, impartial and sincere, and it yields a harvest of righteousness sown in peace. The answer to the tongue is not a technique, but a new source.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not many should become teachers, because teachers are judged more strictly. We all stumble, and the one who controls his speech is mature. The tongue is small, like a bit or a rudder, but it steers everything; like a spark, it sets a forest ablaze. No human can tame it. With it we bless God and curse people made in his likeness, which ought not to be. A spring cannot give fresh and salt water from one opening.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Tongue Cannot Be Tamed

The tongue is small and decisive, and no human can tame it. The problem is the spring, not the water; the answer is wisdom from above.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Too many in the congregation wanted to teach.

Now: We cannot bless God and curse people made in his likeness from the same mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, because we who teach will be judged more strictly.

Too many wanted the job. In a Jewish setting the rabbi was the most honoured figure. In young, unstructured churches, anyone who could hold a room had an opening.

“We who teach”. James puts himself inside the warning. To whom much is given, much is required. A teacher handles souls with words; error from the front does damage private error does not.

The hinge. Teaching is done entirely with the tongue, so the teacher is most exposed to what follows.

What it does not mean. Not discouragement of the gift; the New Testament prizes teaching. It discourages the wanting of a visible role for the sake of standing rather than service.

On a Tuesday. Before volunteering to lead the Bible study, ask honestly: do I want to serve these people, or to be heard? Both may be mixed. Bring the motive to God first.

verseByVerse.quote: For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We all stumble in many ways. Anyone who never stumbles in what he says is mature, able to control his whole body.

We all stumble. The ordinary word for tripping, repeatedly and mostly without intending to. James includes himself.

Speech as a measure. “Perfect” means mature (1:4). Doctrine, zeal and generosity can all be produced by effort or temperament. The tongue is the last thing to come under control. Speech is largely involuntary; it arrives. That makes it honest evidence of the heart (Matthew 12:34).

verseByVerse.quote: If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We put bits into horses’ mouths to make them obey, and turn their whole bodies. Ships, though large and driven by strong winds, are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot wants.

Small and decisive. A half-ton horse turned by a few ounces of iron; a ship in a gale steered by a board at the stern. The tongue is the helm.

Steered. “Wherever the will of the pilot directs.” A rudder does not choose the course; someone’s will is behind it. That is the hopeful note: the question is who has hold of it.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tongue is small, but it boasts of great things. A small spark sets a great forest on fire. The tongue is a fire, a world of evil among our members, corrupting the whole person, setting the whole course of life on fire, and itself set on fire by hell.

From power to danger. Bit and rudder were neutral. Fire is not. One dropped cigarette, and a hillside is gone.

A world of unrighteousness. A universe of wrong in one organ. It stains the whole body and sets the “wheel” of life ablaze.

Set on fire by hell. Gehenna, Jesus’ word for final judgment. Destructive speech has a supply line, and it runs from below.

Why so strong? These refugees were being hurt less by outside persecution than by what they said to each other.

On a Tuesday. One sarcastic comment in a team meeting, one forwarded message, one rumour repeated: the forest can go up from a spark. Before you speak or send, ask whether this word builds up or burns.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here translates Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People have tamed every kind of animal, bird, reptile and sea creature, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

Genesis dominion. The four categories echo Genesis 1. Humanity has broken horses and trained falcons, yet cannot rule six inches of its own mouth.

Absolute. Not “difficult” but impossible, by resolve or technique.

Restless and poisonous. The same word as the unstable man of 1:8. Full of venom, like a snake.

Then what? James is not writing a self-improvement chapter. If effort could tame the tongue, the answer would be effort. He shuts that door. No human can tame it, but God can change the heart from which words come (Matthew 12:34). Pray, “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth” (Psalm 141:3). Fill your heart with God’s word. Think before speaking. When your tongue fails, confess and make it right. The Spirit’s fruit includes self-control (Galatians 5:23). The chapter’s answer is wisdom from above (v. 17).

verseByVerse.quote: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the tongue we praise our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people made in God’s likeness. Praise and cursing come from the same mouth. My brothers and sisters, this should not be.

We. James includes himself again.

Real worship, real cursing. The same mouth was singing an hour ago. These are worshippers, not hypocrites who despise God.

The image of God. We curse people “made in the likeness of God”, as Genesis 1:26 teaches. You cannot bless the original and curse the image. Contempt for people is never small: the likeness remains, however defaced. It covers the difficult neighbour, the political opponent, and the church member who really wronged you.

Is all cursing forbidden? The psalms call down God’s judgment, and Paul calls a false gospel accursed (Galatians 1:8). That leaves judgment to God. What James forbids is cursing people out of malice, in our own name. Jesus says, “bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28).

Gentle at the end. After the fire of v. 6, “these things ought not to be so” is almost soft, and addressed to brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? Can a fig tree bear olives, or a grapevine figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.

Output reveals source. Sweet and brackish springs near the Jordan were well known. Fruit shows the tree (Matthew 7:16–20).

Deal with the spring. Speech is a symptom. Reforming it directly is treating the outflow as the problem.

Impossible. No bitter source yields sweet water now and then. Blessing and cursing from one church shows something wrong at the source.

On a Tuesday. If your words at home are often harsh, do not only resolve to speak more gently. Ask God to show you what is in the spring: resentment, fear, pride. Bring that to the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Who is wise? Let him show it by good conduct done in humility. Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in the heart are not wisdom from above, but earthly, unspiritual and demonic, and they produce disorder and every evil. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere. Peacemakers who sow in peace reap a harvest of righteousness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wisdom Shown, Not Stated

Wisdom is proved by good conduct in meekness. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, and almost every mark of it concerns how we treat others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition lay behind the quarrelling.

Now: The eagerness to be seen as wise is itself evidence against the claim.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show it by his good life, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom.

Back to the would-be teachers. Here is how the claim is tested.

Shown, not stated. Biblical wisdom is skill in living; the Hebrew word is used of craftsmen. The evidence is a life, not an argument. As with faith (2:18), the demand is: show me.

Meekness. Strength under control. The wise man does not need to win the room or be recognised as the wisest. The eagerness to be seen as wise is evidence against the claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you harbour bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast about it or deny the truth. Such “wisdom” does not come from heaven; it is earthly, unspiritual and demonic. Where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there is disorder and every evil practice.

The source found. Bitter jealousy: zeal for a cause curdled into zeal against a person. Selfish ambition: a word from hired political canvassing, working a crowd for your own advancement. Both are “in your hearts”: the spring of v. 11.

Three steps down. Earthly: reaches no higher than this world. Unspiritual: natural, without the Spirit. Demonic: the same source as the tongue set on fire by hell (v. 6).

Disorder. Private ambition produces public chaos, which makes room for everything else.

On a Tuesday. A church split often begins not with doctrine but with two people who want the same role. Ask whether there is someone whose success you secretly resent. Name it before God, and pray for their good.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the wisdom from heaven is first pure, then peace-loving, considerate, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere. Peacemakers who sow in peace reap a harvest of righteousness.

From above. Like every good gift (1:17), and given to anyone who asks (1:5).

First pure. First in priority. Purity comes before peace, which forbids the false peace that keeps quiet about sin.

Then peaceable. Gentle: not insisting on every last right. Open to reason: willing to be persuaded, exactly what the quarrelling teachers lacked. Full of mercy and good fruits. Impartial: back to the gold ring. Sincere: without a mask, the opposite of double-mindedness.

Not intellectual. Almost every mark concerns how we treat people.

Sown in peace. The chapter that opened with fire closes with sowing. Fire destroys in an afternoon; a harvest grows slowly. Peacemakers do not just avoid conflict; they make peace, which is work.

For worship. This list is a portrait of Christ, the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Ask him for it today.

4.title: Submit to God: Pride, the World, and the Brevity of Life
4.overview:
Chapter 4 goes to the root of the church’s failures. Quarrels come from desires at war within each person. Those desires come from friendship with the world, which is spiritual adultery against God. The remedy is humble submission: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, grieve over sin, humble yourselves. At the centre stands Proverbs 3:34: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” And “he gives more grace.”

The chapter ends with two warnings against taking God’s place: judging a brother, which sets us over the law, and planning as if tomorrow were ours, which forgets that we are a mist. The humble say, “If the Lord wills.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Quarrels, Adultery, and More Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your fights come from desires at war inside you. You want and do not have, so you quarrel; you do not ask, or you ask to feed your desires. Friendship with the world is hostility to God. But God yearns jealously over us, and gives more grace: he opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. So submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse your hands and hearts, grieve over sin, and humble yourselves, and he will lift you up.
verseByVerse.theology:
But He Gives More Grace

Quarrels come from desires at war within us, and friendship with the world is spiritual adultery. Yet God gives more grace — to the humble.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers prayed, but to fund the very desires that divided them.

Now: Submit to God, resist the devil, draw near — and he will draw near to you.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What causes fights and quarrels among you? Is it not your desires battling inside you? You want something but do not get it, so you kill. You covet but cannot have, so you quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask God.

The war within. “Passions” is hēdonai, pleasures. The war is not first between factions but inside each person. Settle the presenting issue, and a person at war inside will find another.

“Murder”. Some have proposed reading “envy”, but the manuscripts do not support it. James is tracing sin to its root as Jesus did: hatred is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22). He is naming where desire is heading.

Desire, frustration, violence. The pattern twice. Thwarted desire is what sets the room on fire.

You do not ask. After all the heat, the simplest sentence. They organised life around getting, and never asked the God who gives generously (1:5).

On a Tuesday. Next time you are angry with your spouse or colleague, ask: what do I want that I am not getting? Then take that desire to God before you take it out on them.

verseByVerse.quote: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, to spend it on your pleasures.

Praying to fund appetite. “Spend” is the word for the prodigal squandering his inheritance. These people are praying, but prayer has become a means of financing the desires that divide them.

Mercy in refusal. A father who funded every appetite would be negligent, not generous. God’s “no” here is kindness.

A searching question. When a prayer goes unanswered for years, ask not only “Why is God silent?” but also “What would I do with it if I got it?” This does not apply to genuine need, which James tells them to bring to God. It applies to desire.

verseByVerse.quote: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hatred towards God? Anyone who chooses to be a friend of the world becomes God’s enemy.

Adulteresses. The Greek is feminine: the prophets’ language for Israel as an unfaithful bride (Hosea, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). Quarrels and greed are not just bad behaviour; they are a marriage being broken.

The world. Not the planet or its people, whom God loves, but life organised without God.

No middle. Friendship with the world does not merely lead to enmity; it is enmity.

What it does not mean. Not that enjoying good things or living among unbelievers is sin. God gives every good gift (1:17). It is about where the heart’s affection points. The wishing is the adultery.

Makes himself. He has taken up a position. That is why grace can still reach him.
verseByVerse.note: The prophets called Israel’s unfaithfulness to God “adultery.”

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”? But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think Scripture says without reason that God jealously longs for the spirit he made to live in us? But he gives more grace. That is why it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

A hard verse. Verse 5 is difficult to translate, and no single Old Testament verse matches it; James seems to summarise a biblical theme. The ESV reading, that God yearns jealously over the spirit he gave us, fits the adultery of v. 4. Some read the spirit as the Holy Spirit, who yearns over us. Either way, God will not share us with the world.

Holy jealousy. Not pettiness, but a husband’s right response to a wife who is leaving. A God who felt nothing at our unfaithfulness would love us less, not more. Indifference is the opposite of love.

More grace. The turning point of the letter. Greater than the adultery, the quarrels, the appetite. Whatever sin has cost, the supply is larger.

Downhill. Grace flows down. “Opposes” is military: God lines up against the proud.

For worship. “But he gives more grace” is worth memorising. Say it whenever your sin seems bigger than God’s mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 5 is hard to translate; the ESV margin offers other readings. No single Old Testament verse matches it; it seems to sum up Scripture’s teaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So submit to God. Resist the devil, and he will run from you. Come near to God, and he will come near to you. Wash your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.

Ten commands. Verses 7–10 hold ten imperatives, all unpacking “the humble”.

Submit first. A military word: arrange yourself under. Only then resist. A man who has not submitted to God has no standing from which to resist anything.

He will flee. Not a long siege. The devil cannot stand against a believer submitted to God.

How to resist. By standing firm in faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), putting on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:11–17), and answering lies with God’s word, as Jesus did (Matthew 4:1–11). Not by shouting at Satan or using formulas; even the archangel said only, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9).

Draw near. The priest’s word for approaching the altar. God is not waiting far off; he already yearns over us. Think of the father who ran (Luke 15:20).

Hands and hearts. Outward conduct and inward loyalty. And “double-minded” at last receives its remedy: purification, after “he gives more grace”.

On a Tuesday. When a familiar temptation comes, do three things: submit (“Lord, I am yours”), resist (say no, and quote a verse), draw near (pray for a minute). The order matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grieve, mourn and weep. Change your laughter to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.

A call to repentance. The letter began, “Count it all joy”. So why gloom? Because these people were quarrelling and coveting cheerfully. The laughter to be turned to mourning is the laughter of people not taking their sin seriously.

What it does not mean. Not permanent gloom or misery as a spiritual state. It is godly grief, which “produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10), and leads to joy.

Who does what. The humbling is ours; the lifting is God’s. That is the reverse of our default, where we exalt ourselves and hope God will not humble us. It is the pattern of Christ (Philippians 2:8–9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not slander one another. Judging a brother sets you over the law instead of under it; there is one Lawgiver and Judge. And do not plan as though tomorrow were yours. You are a mist. Say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” Boasting about the future is evil, and whoever knows the right thing to do and does not do it, sins.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sin as Knowledge Not Acted On

Speaking against a brother sets us over the law instead of under it. And whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The merchants' plan was complete except for God.

Now: Plan, but hold every plan under “if the Lord wills” — life itself included.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not slander one another. Whoever speaks against a brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. If you judge the law, you are not keeping it but sitting in judgment on it. There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, who can save and destroy. Who are you to judge your neighbour?

Speak against. From slander to the accurate but damaging remark: the tongue of chapter 3 turned on the church.

Judging the law. The law says love your neighbour (2:8). Condemning him sets that law aside, ruling it does not apply here. A judge stands over the law; a doer stands under it.

One Judge. Only one can act on the verdict either way.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians may never judge. We test teaching (1 John 4:1), and the church exercises discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What is forbidden is slander, and condemning a brother as if we were his final judge.

Neighbour. The last word brings back Leviticus 19:18. The person you are judging is the one you were commanded to love.

On a Tuesday. In a conversation about an absent church member, ask yourself: would I say this to his face, in love? If not, change the subject, or pray for him instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now listen, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this city, spend a year there, do business and make money.” You do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Instead you should say, “If it is the Lord’s will, we will live and do this or that.”

A complete plan. Timing, destination, duration, activity, outcome. Nothing wrong with any of it. Trade, profit and planning are not condemned (Proverbs 6:6–8).

What is missing. One clause. The plan assumes knowledge no one has.

A mist. The haze over a field that is gone when the sun is up: not a short life, but a brief appearance.

If the Lord wills. James does not cancel the trip. He adds the clause, and it covers living as well as doing.

What it does not mean. Not a formula to tack onto sentences. One person can say the words with no real dependence; another can plan the whole year in that spirit without saying them once.

On a Tuesday. As you put next year’s holiday in the diary, pause and pray: “Lord, if you will, we will live and go.” David’s prayer is ours: “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15).

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is, you boast in your arrogant plans. All such boasting is evil. So anyone who knows the good he ought to do and does not do it, sins.

Arrogance. The word first described a travelling quack claiming powers he did not have.

Evil. Not naive but evil: a mist claiming the knowledge and control that belong to God.

Sin as omission. “So” ties v. 17 to the passage: now they know about the mist and “if the Lord wills”. Sin is not only doing what is forbidden, but not doing what is known to be right.

The whole letter in one sentence. The hearer who does not do (1:22), the speaker who does not give (2:16), the one who knows and does not act. James never charges them with ignorance, but with being informed.

On a Tuesday. Every sermon understood and every book agreed with raises the stakes. Pick one thing you already know you should do, and do it today.
