5.title: Patient Until He Comes: Wealth, Endurance, and Prayer
5.overview:
The final chapter of James brings together the letter’s major themes in a conclusion that moves from prophetic warning to pastoral tenderness. The opening passage (vv. 1–6) is the most severe in the letter: a woe oracle against the wealthy who have oppressed the poor, withheld wages, and lived in luxury while the righteous suffer. This is not a general warning about the spiritual dangers of wealth; it is a specific indictment of wealthy oppressors who have used their power against the most vulnerable, and whose judgment is certain.

Against this dark background, the letter turns to the suffering community with pastoral warmth. The patience of the farmer who waits for the rains (vv. 7–11) is the model: you cannot hurry the harvest; you can only wait, watching for the rains, knowing that the harvest is coming. The coming of the Lord is the horizon that makes patience possible — not resignation to injustice but confidence that the Judge is at the door and that he will make all things right. The examples of the prophets and of Job encourage: those who endured affliction under the old covenant discovered the compassion and mercy of the Lord on the other side.

The letter ends where the Christian life begins and always returns: prayer. The prayer of a righteous person has great power (v. 16). Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and his prayer shut and opened the rain. The community of prayer is the community that is simultaneously most realistic about its need (confessing sins to one another) and most confident about its resource (the God who hears and acts). And the final word of the letter is not about doctrine or practice but about people: if any one among you wanders, and someone brings them back, they have covered a multitude of sins. The community that prays together is the community that reaches for the wanderer — and that reaching is, James says, one of the greatest works of grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries coming on you (v.1). Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten (v.2); your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire — you have laid up treasure in the last days (v.3).

Behold, the wages of the labourers who mowed your fields, kept back by fraud, are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts (v.4). You have lived in luxury and self-indulgence, fattening your hearts in a day of slaughter (v.5). You have condemned and murdered the righteous person, and he does not resist you (v.6).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rust That Testifies

Hoarded wealth will testify against those who kept back the wages of their labourers. The cries of the harvesters have reached the Lord of hosts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A day-labourer's withheld wage meant a family without supper.

Now: Comfort bought by someone else's hunger is not a blessing but fattening for a day of slaughter.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Come now, you rich, weep and howl.” The verb is violent — to shriek, the noise of open grief. This is prophetic denunciation in the manner of Amos, and it is worth noting that James is almost certainly not addressing members of the congregation here. He addresses the oppressors directly, as the prophets did, while the oppressed listen.

“For the miseries that are coming upon you.” Not that have come. The judgement is future and certain, and the weeping is commanded now on account of it.

Then three assets, in ascending order of durability, and all three have failed. “Your riches have rotted” — the general word, and rot is what happens to grain and produce. “Your garments are moth-eaten” — fine clothing was stored wealth in that world, and a moth needs no thief. “Your gold and silver have corroded.”

That third one is chemically impossible, and James knows it. Gold does not corrode; that is precisely why it has been money for five thousand years. He is making a point by overstatement: the one asset that cannot decay has decayed. Nothing they own has survived.

“And their corrosion will be evidence against you.” The word is a legal term — testimony for the prosecution. The rust is a witness, and what it testifies to is that the wealth sat unused. Metal that is spent does not corrode. This corroded because it was hoarded while the men who earned it went hungry.

“And will eat your flesh like fire.” The image turns on them bodily: the corrosion that consumed the treasure will consume the owner.

“You have laid up treasure in the last days.” That is the final irony. They were accumulating in the very period when it could least be of use — like a man buying property in a town he knows is to be flooded. The folly is not the wealth. It is the timing.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the specific charge, and it is not vague: “the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud.”

The Old Testament is explicit about this. A hired man was to be paid the same day, before sunset, because he is poor and counting on it (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14–15). A day-labourer had no savings; the wage bought that evening’s food. To withhold it overnight was not a cashflow decision. It was a family going without supper.

“Are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.” Two cries: the wages themselves cry, and so do the men. The image is the one used of Abel’s blood crying from the ground (Gen 4:10), and “Lord of hosts” is the military title — the LORD of armies. James chooses it deliberately. The defrauded workers have no advocate, no court and no standing. Their case has been heard by the commander of heaven’s armies.

“You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence.” The two words are soft living and wanton pleasure, and the contrast is the whole point — this luxury was funded by that unpaid wage. James is not condemning wealth in the abstract but a specific transfer: comfort at one table bought by hunger at another.

“You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.” A terrible image. The beast is grazing contentedly, and it does not know what the day is for. They took their prosperity as evidence of favour; James says it was fattening.

“You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.” Condemned is a courtroom word — the machinery of law used against a man who could not afford it (cf. 2:6). And the last sentence is the most terrible: he is not resisting. There was never a contest.
verseByVerse.note: The Law required day-labourers to be paid the same day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–20 — Patience, Prayer, and Going After the Wanderer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Be patient until the coming of the Lord, as the farmer waits for the early and late rains (v.7); establish your hearts, for his coming is at hand (v.8). Do not grumble against one another — the Judge is standing at the door (v.9). Take the prophets as an example of suffering and patience (v.10); we call those blessed who remained steadfast, and you have heard of Job and seen the Lord’s purpose, how he is compassionate and merciful (v.11). Above all, do not swear, but let your yes be yes and your no be no (v.12).

Suffering? Pray. Cheerful? Sing praise (v.13). Sick? Call the elders to pray over him and anoint him with oil (v.14); the prayer of faith will save him and the Lord will raise him up, and if he has sinned he will be forgiven (v.15). So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, for a righteous person’s prayer has great power in its working (v.16) — Elijah, a man of like nature with us, prayed and it did not rain for three and a half years (v.17), and prayed again and the heavens gave rain (v.18).

Finally: if anyone wanders from the truth and someone brings him back (v.19), let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save a soul from death and cover a multitude of sins (v.20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prayer of Faith

Be patient as the farmer waits for the rains, because the Lord is coming. Pray in every condition; the prayer of faith is prayer submitted to God's will, and Elijah was a man like us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Pressed from outside, the congregation was grumbling against one another.

Now: The letter ends by sending ordinary believers after the one who has wandered.

verseByVerse.quote: Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Be patient, therefore, brothers.” The address changes back to the congregation, and everything softens. The word is not the hypomone of chapter 1, which is endurance under weight. It is makrothymia — long-tempered, slow to burn, the patience shown toward difficult people.

Which is exactly right after verses 1–6. Having heard their oppressors denounced, the natural next move is to take matters up themselves. James says: wait.

“Until the coming of the Lord.” And that is the ground of it. He is not telling them the injustice does not matter or that it will resolve itself. He has just said the Lord of hosts has heard. The waiting is not for nothing to happen; it is for someone else to act.

“See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth… until it receives the early and the late rains.” The picture is precisely local. Palestinian agriculture depends on autumn rains to soften the ground for sowing and spring rains to swell the grain before harvest, and between them lie months in which nothing can be done.

The farmer’s patience is not passivity — he has ploughed and sown, and he will reap. But there is a stretch in the middle where all the activity in the world would not bring the harvest forward by a day, and the mark of a farmer is that he knows it.

“Establish your hearts” — the word means to make firm, to prop. Waiting is not merely refraining; it requires something to be shored up.

Was James wrong, since two thousand years have passed? At hand means that Christ’s coming is the next great event in God’s plan and could come at any time, not that it would come within a few years. Peter answers the same objection: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and his delay is patience, giving time for repentance (2 Pet 3:8–9).

“For the coming of the Lord is at hand.” Not far off. That is the whole reason the waiting is bearable, and it should be said plainly that James expected it soon. The New Testament’s consistent posture is imminence — not a date, but a nearness that makes patience reasonable rather than resigned.
verseByVerse.note: In Israel the early rain came in autumn, at sowing, and the late rain in spring, before harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not grumble against one another, brothers.” The word means to groan or sigh — and it is not the sound of open quarrelling but of muttering. The complaint under the breath, the remark to one person about another.

The placing is shrewd. James has just told them to be patient toward their oppressors — and he knows exactly where that pressure goes. Pressure from outside that cannot be discharged outward is discharged sideways, onto the people nearest. A congregation under strain from without turns on itself, and the form it takes is rarely dramatic. It is grumbling.

“So that you may not be judged.” The warning connects directly to 4:11–12, where judging a brother usurped the one Lawgiver’s office. To grumble is to pass sentence privately, and the man who convenes his own court will find himself in somebody else’s.

“Behold, the Judge is standing at the door.” It is one of the most vivid sentences in the letter, and it does two things at once.

It is a comfort. The oppressed of verses 1–6 are told their Judge has not merely heard the case — he has arrived at the building.

And it is a warning to the same people in the same breath. He is at the door of their room too, and he is about to walk in on the muttering. James gives them no opportunity to enjoy the judgement of their enemies without noticing where they are standing themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.”

The choice is pointed. The prophets were not men who suffered despite their faithfulness; they suffered because of it, and specifically because they spoke in the Lord’s name. James is telling a congregation being oppressed for their faith that they are in the succession, not the exception.

“Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast.” And here the word returns to hypomone, the endurance of chapter 1 — and to “blessed”, which picks up 1:12 exactly. The letter is closing its own circle.

“You have heard of the steadfastness of Job.” The example repays thought, because Job was not patient in the sense the phrase has acquired in English. He protested at length, demanded an audience, and told God he had a case to argue. What he did was not let go — which is what hypomone means. James’s idea of steadfastness plainly has room for a man who complains bitterly and will not walk away.

“And you have seen the purpose of the Lord.” The phrase means the end, the outcome — how it turned out. Job could not see it from inside; the reader of the book can, and that is the advantage James is handing them.

“How the Lord is compassionate and merciful.” That is a remarkable conclusion to draw from the book of Job, which contains no explanation of his suffering at all. James does not say the Lord explained himself. He says the end of the story showed what he was like — and the two words he chooses are the ancient self-description of God at Sinai (Exod 34:6).

verseByVerse.quote: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But above all, my brothers, do not swear.” The phrase is arresting. Above all what? Not the whole letter — James can hardly mean this matters more than faith and works. It is most likely a way of flagging a final point of importance, and it echoes his brother almost word for word (Matt 5:34–37).

The oath-taking in view is not courtroom testimony, and it is not blasphemy. It is the habit of reinforcing your own speech: swearing by heaven, by earth, by the temple, by your own head — a graded system in which some oaths were held binding and others were understood to be escape routes.

That is what makes it a speech problem rather than a religious one, and it belongs to a letter that has said so much about the tongue. A man who must swear to be believed has admitted that his ordinary word is not reliable.

“But let your ‘yes’ be yes and your ‘no’ be no.” The remedy is not more solemn language but less. If a man’s plain word holds, he needs no machinery to prop it up — and the machinery is itself evidence that something is wrong.

“So that you may not fall under condemnation.” The stakes are higher than the subject seems to warrant, and that is the point. A graded oath system is a device for deceiving while appearing truthful, and God is not deceived by the gradations.

Does this forbid all oaths, even in court or at a wedding? Quakers and many Anabaptists have held that it does. But God himself swears by himself (Heb 6:13–17), Paul calls God as witness (Rom 1:9; 2 Cor 1:23), and Jesus answered when put under oath (Matt 26:63–64). The Reformed confessions therefore allow solemn and lawful oaths. What James forbids is casual swearing, oaths used to make some words binding and others not. A Christian’s plain word should be enough.

The practical question this puts is small and searching. Do the people who know you best need you to insist? A person whose word is simply good has no use for emphasis, and the habit of over-assurance is usually a sign that somewhere the plain word has stopped being enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions in quick succession, each with a one-word answer, and together they map the whole emotional range of a Christian life onto prayer and praise.

“Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray.” The word covers hardship generally — the same root as the “suffering” of the prophets in verse 10. And the response is not resignation, not stoicism, and not a search for the reason. Pray.

“Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.” And that is the half we habitually neglect. Most Christians know that trouble should send them to God; far fewer treat gladness as equally directional.

The pairing is the point. There is no condition in which the answer is to do nothing God-ward. Trouble goes up as prayer, joy goes up as song, and between them they cover every day anybody has.

It is also a quiet correction of a besetting error, which is to treat God as an emergency service. A man who prays only when suffering has a relationship with his own need rather than with God — and the second question is there to expose it.

And note that James does not require the cheerful man to become solemn before he approaches. The gladness itself is what goes up. This is the same writer who told them to count trials joy and to let laughter turn to mourning when repenting — he is not against any emotion. He is against every emotion being kept to oneself.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church.” Note who initiates: the sick man calls. And note the plural — not the gifted individual but the elders, the ordinary appointed leadership of the local congregation.

“And let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.” The main verb is pray; the anointing is a participle, subordinate to it. Oil in that world was both medicine (the Samaritan poured oil on the wounds, Luke 10:34) and a sign of consecration. Whether the gesture here is chiefly medical or symbolic, it is not the operative thing — the praying is, and it is done “in the name of the Lord.”

“And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up.”

This has to be handled honestly, because read flatly it promises that every believing prayer heals, and every Christian knows it does not. Several things keep it from meaning that. The letter itself has just said that asking can be answered no when the asking is wrong (4:3). Paul prayed three times about his thorn and was refused (2 Cor 12:8–9), and left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Tim 4:20). And “the prayer of faith” is not prayer accompanied by sufficient confidence — faith of that kind would be a work, and its absence would make the sick man’s illness his own fault, which is precisely the cruelty this verse has often been used to inflict.

Better to take it as prayer offered in submission to God’s will, which is what faith always is in this letter — and the verbs support it. “Save” and “raise up” are both words with a larger reach than physical recovery, and the final raising up is guaranteed for every believer whether or not this illness ends.

Is this the basis for the Roman Catholic sacrament of the anointing of the sick, once given mainly to the dying as last rites? James speaks of anointing the sick to pray for their recovery, the Lord will raise him up, not to prepare them for death, and the healing comes from the prayer and the Lord, not from a sacrament.

Should churches still anoint with oil? The oil was used in the ancient world both as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God; here, with prayer in the Lord’s name, it is most likely a sign. Elders may still pray over the sick and anoint them, and this does not oppose medicine; Christians should use doctors and pray. God often heals, but not always; Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Tim 4:20).

“And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.” The conditional is careful and merciful. James allows that sin may be involved and refuses to assume it — which is exactly the balance Job’s friends failed to keep.
verseByVerse.note: Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.”

The “therefore” follows the conditional clause about sin. Since sin may sometimes lie behind trouble, deal with it — and deal with it in the open.

Note the direction: to one another. Not to a priest, and not to God only. James is describing something mutual and horizontal — ordinary Christians telling each other the truth about themselves. It requires no office and it is available in any congregation, and it is almost universally avoided.

The reason it is avoided is the reason it works. Sin kept private grows in the dark and is fed by the fear of exposure; the man who has told somebody has already lost the thing that was protecting it. And the pairing matters — confession alone leaves a person exposed, so James joins it to intercession. You tell someone, and they pray for you.

“The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.” The last phrase is difficult and probably means in its working — that is, prayer is not a stored potency but something powerful in operation, effective as it is being prayed.

Healing here includes the whole person, the body in v. 15 and the soul restored through confession. And not every sickness comes from sin; James says if he has committed sins (v. 15), and Jesus denied that the man born blind suffered for anyone’s sin (John 9:3).

And “righteous” should not be read as a rare spiritual class, or the whole verse becomes a discouragement to the very people it is written for. The next verse settles it decisively: the righteous man James has in mind is Elijah, and the first thing he says about him is that he was made of exactly the same stuff we are.

verseByVerse.quote: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Elijah was a man with a nature like ours.” James puts that first, before anything about the miracle, and it is the whole reason he chose the example.

Elijah is the most spectacular figure in the prophetic history — fire from heaven on Carmel, the ravens, the chariot. He is exactly the man a discouraged congregation would cite as proof that prayer works for other people. So James disarms the objection in the first clause: same nature, same stuff.

And the account bears him out. This is the prophet who, immediately after the greatest answered prayer in the Old Testament, ran into the desert and asked God to let him die (1 Kgs 19:4). Whatever Elijah was, he was not temperamentally immune to despair.

“And he prayed fervently that it might not rain.” The Greek is a Hebrew idiom — literally he prayed with prayer — which conveys earnestness. And notice that 1 Kings does not actually record him praying for the drought; it records him announcing it. James, or the tradition he knows, understands the announcement to have rested on prayer — which says something about where a prophet’s public word comes from.

“And for three years and six months it did not rain.” The Lord gives the same figure (Luke 4:25).

“Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.” Both directions — the withholding and the giving — came through the same channel. And the closing image is agricultural, which returns to the farmer of verse 7 waiting for the early and late rains. The letter’s pictures are tying themselves together as it ends.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah’s prayers are implied in 1 Kings; Jesus also gives the drought’s length as three and a half years.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter ends without a benediction, without greetings, without a signature. It simply stops — on the subject of somebody else’s soul.

“If anyone among you wanders from the truth.” The verb is to be led astray, to go off course — the same root as our “planet”, the wandering star. It is drift, not a decision. Nobody announces that they are leaving.

“And someone brings him back.” Note how ordinary that someone is. Not the elders of verse 14, not a teacher, not an office. Someone — anyone who notices and goes after him.

“Let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death.” That is as high a claim as could be made for a piece of personal pastoral work, and it is made about an unnamed church member.

“And will cover a multitude of sins” — an echo of Proverbs 10:12. The covering is God’s work; the human agent is the occasion of it, not the cause. Whose sins are covered is left slightly open, and probably deliberately: the man restored is forgiven, and the one who went after him has been doing the very thing this whole letter has demanded, which is to be a doer.

And that is a fitting last word. James has spent five chapters insisting that faith shows, that hearing is not doing, that religion is visited widows and unstained lives, and that the tongue reveals the heart. He ends by describing the most concrete act of love available to an ordinary Christian: noticing that someone has stopped coming, and going to find out why.

Whose soul, and what death? The one who wanders is saved from eternal death by being brought back, and his many sins are covered by God’s forgiveness. Can a true believer wander so far as to be lost? Arminian Christians read the verse that way. The more likely reading is that the wanderer is either a believer whom God restores through the loving pursuit of others, or a professing member whose wandering would have shown that his faith was never real. Either way, the person who brings him back is God’s means of keeping him, which is why we must not leave wanderers alone.

No farewell. Just a man walking out to look for somebody.
